stops.name: Kansas City, Missouri: born in a newspaperman's house
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Birth date, birth name and Kansas City are given by Wikipedia, 'Ted Shawn'. The deaths of the elder brother and of the mother about eight months apart, and the boarding-house years after, come from the NYPL Ted Shawn Papers biographical note as relayed through the research dossier; I did not re-fetch that finding aid myself, so the 1903 sequence is reconstruction here, not attestation. The parents' names follow the Wikipedia article.
stops.campa: Edwin Myers Shawn is born in Kansas City on the twenty-first of October 1891, second son of the newspaperman Ellsworth Shawn and Mary Lee Booth Shawn, christened Edwin though the world will know him as Ted. The house does not last. His elder brother dies, his mother dies about eight months later, and the boy and his father move from one boarding house to another with the furniture of a family behind them. Two things survive the dispersal: the Methodist religion of the household, which points him toward a pulpit, and his father's trade in words, which he takes up himself and works at for sixty years.
suggested_refs: The Ted Shawn Papers, New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, Jerome Robbins Dance Division (archives.nypl.org/dan/19667)
sources: NYPL, Ted Shawn Papers finding aid, biographical note (relayed through the research dossier, not independently re-fetched)

stops.name: University of Denver: the third year of the ministry
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction on the dating. The NYPL chronology states that he was in his third year of studying for the ministry at the University of Denver when he contracted diphtheria, which puts the enrolment around 1908 or 1909 rather than at 1911, the year the research dossier originally attached to it. The dossier itself flagged that internal inconsistency and left it open; the correction resolves in favour of the illness interrupting a course already three years old. Month and day are unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He enrols at the University of Denver to prepare for the Methodist ministry, around 1908 or 1909, and gets three years into the course. The training is not wasted. The cadence of the pulpit stays in his prose, and the conviction that the body is an instrument of worship, which no seminary teaches him, is argued for the rest of his life in books with titles like Gods Who Dance. He does not finish the degree. He is in his third year when he falls ill.

stops.name: Denver: diphtheria, and Hazel Wallack's studio
stops.date_confidence: The illness, the temporary lower-body paralysis, the age of about nineteen and the therapeutic study with Hazel Wallack, a former Metropolitan Opera dancer, are attested by Wikipedia, 'Ted Shawn'. The month is unknown and defaulted. The popular framing that dance cured the paralysis is a conversion narrative Shawn himself propagated and is carried here as his telling, not as a clinical finding. Denver coordinates inherited byte-identical from ruth_st_denis.journey.json.
stops.campa: At about nineteen he contracts diphtheria, and the illness leaves him with temporary paralysis of the lower body. He begins studying with Hazel Wallack, a former Metropolitan Opera dancer working in Denver, as therapy: ballet positions taken slowly, for the legs, in a room with a barre. He will spend fifty years telling this story, and in the telling it hardens into a conversion in which dance itself performs the cure. No clinical record supports that. What the record has is a ministry student in a rented Denver studio, doing ballet positions at a barre for the sake of his legs.
suggested_refs: Hazel Wallack's Denver studio, the first dance training Shawn received

stops.name: Denver: The Incense
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested through both Shawn's own account in Ruth St. Denis: Pioneer and Prophet and the corresponding stop in ruth_st_denis.journey.json; the month and day of the performance are not established by any source reached. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from ruth_st_denis.journey.json, segment 'Denver: Ted Shawn in the house'. Nothing about the encounter is mutual and nothing is recorded on her side.
stops.campa: Ruth St. Denis brings her Oriental cycle to Denver, and Shawn, nineteen or twenty, buys a seat. She is already internationally known. He is a lapsed ministry student with a barre habit. He watches The Incense, a solo in which a woman offers smoke to a god with her arms, and he weeps in a full house. He will not meet her for three more years, and nothing about the evening is mutual: she does not know he exists. The date he gives for his own beginning as an artist is this one.
stops.quote: But when I saw The Incense I wept, not caring that it was in a crowded theatre—and never before, or since, have I known so true a religious experience or so poignant a revelation of perfect beauty. I date my own artistic birth from that night.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, Ruth St. Denis: Pioneer and Prophet (San Francisco: John Howell, 1920), ch. IV
suggested_refs: Ruth St. Denis's solo The Incense (1906), the piece Shawn saw in Denver

stops.campa: He travels east to find Ruth St. Denis and does find her, carrying an introduction and an ambition he does not disguise. She takes him as pupil, then partner, then manager of her affairs. On the thirteenth of April the two of them open a tour of the southern United States together, four months before there is a marriage to explain it. The wooing and the booking are the same activity. stops.campa: On the thirteenth of August 1914 Ted Shawn marries Ruth St. Denis. He is twenty-two, she is thirty-five and the more famous by an enormous margin. No source reached names the city or the room where the ceremony takes place; the date is fixed and nothing else about the day is. What the marriage is from the first hour is a firm: two names that will be printed together on bills, on schools, on letterheads. They separate as artists and as a household in the early 1930s and they never divorce. She dies in 1968 still his wife.
stops.quote: I have always worshiped Ruth St. Denis as an artist but I find she is even greater as a woman.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, Ruth St. Denis: Pioneer and Prophet (1920), 'Some Reasons for the Making of this Book'

stops.name: Portland, Oregon: the two names fuse on a bill
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia, 'Denishawn': a theatre manager's naming contest at a Portland performance produced 'The Denishawn Rose Mazurka', and the shortened form became the official identity of school and company. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from ruth_st_denis.journey.json, segment 'Portland, Oregon: the two names fuse on a bill'.
stops.campa: On the sixth of February 1915, on tour in Portland, a theatre manager runs a naming contest for a new mazurka. The winning entry welds the two stage names into one word: Denishawn. It begins as a billing convenience, a way to fit a married double act into a line of type. Within months it is the name of a school, and within a decade the name of the only American institution training dancers in a curriculum nobody else offers. Nobody records who won the contest, or what the prize was.

stops.name: 600 St. Paul Avenue, Los Angeles: the school opens under her name

stops.campa: In the summer of 1915 the school opens in a Spanish-style house at 600 St. Paul Avenue, with an indoor studio, a swimming pool and a tennis court. Its title on the door is the Ruth St. Denis School of Dancing and Its Related Arts; Shawn's half of the compound word is not on the sign yet. The curriculum is his synthesis as much as hers: ballet technique, the expressive system of François Delsarte, music visualization, yoga, and theatrical dances labelled Oriental. Students live on the premises. It is the first American institution of its kind.
stops.quote: Ruth St. Denis has never sacrificed art to antics. She has upheld her own high standard against pressure of all sorts.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, Ruth St. Denis: Pioneer and Prophet (1920), 'Some Reasons for the Making of this Book'

stops.campa: Martha Graham enrols in the school's second summer, twenty-two and late to start. St. Denis takes little interest in her. Shawn does, and keeps her, and four years later builds Xochitl on her, the role that makes her a name. She spends the rest of her life dismantling everything Denishawn taught her and never fully renounces the debt. Doris Humphrey comes through the same door the following year. Jose Limon, a decade further on, learns his craft at two removes from this house, through Humphrey and Charles Weidman, without ever studying with Shawn himself.

stops.campa: Shawn choreographs Invocation to the Thunderbird and dances it himself in a feathered headdress, one item in a Native American repertory built from ethnological reading, museum cases and theatrical instinct. stops.campa: John Howell of San Francisco prints Shawn's first book, Ruth St. Denis: Pioneer and Prophet, Being a History of Her Cycle of Oriental Dances. It is biography, advocacy and company myth in one binding, written by the husband who is also the manager, about the wife who is also the property. He will publish for another thirty-four years, arguing the same case in book after book: that dance is worship, and that America needs its own. He states his reason for this one at the front of it, without embarrassment.
stops.quote: I, because of my love for her and my intense admiration for her creative genius, feel that there should be some record made

stops.name: Tokyo: the postures of the gods, taught first
stops.date_confidence: Japan is attested as a country on the tour; Tokyo and April 1926 are inherited from ruth_st_denis.journey.json and are reconstruction. The quote is verbatim from the 1929 Gods Who Dance, fetched in full text from archive.org, and is used here on the 1926 stop that supplied its material: the observation is dated to the tour by subject, not by any statement in the book placing it in a named school or city, and Shawn records neither.
stops.campa: Japan, and the last long leg of the tour. Shawn goes into training schools and dance houses and sees something he will quote for the rest of his life: that Japanese children are taught the postures of gods and goddesses before they are taught anything else. It is his whole argument handed to him in a classroom, that dance begins in religion and only afterward becomes an art. He writes it down, and three years later it is in print. He does not record the name of the school, or the city, or who told him.
stops.quote: The very first training given to a beginning class in a Japanese dancing school is the postures of the Gods and Goddesses, thus, even in actual practice, starting the dance at always its true source,—religion.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, Gods Who Dance (New York: E. P. Dutton, 1929)

segments.name: The Books, and the End of the Institution

stops.name: New York: The American Ballet, and its argument
stops.date_confidence: Only the year is attested: New York, Henry Holt, 1926, from the standard bibliographic record, with the full text fetched from archive.org (identifier americanballet0000teds). Month and day are unknown and defaulted to 1 January per convention, which places the book earlier in the calendar than the tour's May 1926 close in the preceding segment; the ordering of the two segments should not be read as an ordering of months. The quote is the whole of Shawn's sentence: the research pool carried a spliced version that joined two sentences across an intervening passage about Russians, and that splice is not used here.
stops.campa: Henry Holt publishes The American Ballet, Shawn's manifesto for a national dance. The argument is nationalist and explicit: American dancers, American composers, American designers, American money, on the model by which the Russians made a Russian ballet out of Italian and French training. Alongside it runs a social-evolutionary racial scheme that later scholarship reads as eugenic. He does not bury that in footnotes or leave it to inference; it is on the page in the same voice as everything else, in a book written to persuade.
stops.quote: And if we are going to have a great American Ballet, it will have to be on the same basis: American born and American trained dancers, dancing to music by American composers, with scenery and costumes designed by American artists, and under the direction and management of American business men of great vision.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, The American Ballet (New York: Henry Holt, 1926)

Dutton publishes Gods Who Dance, the book the Asian tour was gathering material for: a comparative religious history of the art, arguing that every people's dancing begins in worship and that America's ought to as well. The first chapter states the premise without hedging.

stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Jacob's Pillow' gives the acquisition flatly as 1931, correcting the research pool's '1930-1931'; the month is unknown and defaulted. The name origin, Jacob Carter III settling the land in 1790, the switchback called Jacob's Ladder and the pillow-shaped boulder, is attested there. stops.campa: He buys an abandoned hill farm on George Carter Road in the Berkshires, up a switchback the locals call Jacob's Ladder. The name Jacob's Pillow is already on the property when he arrives, carried down from Jacob Carter III, who settled the land in 1790, and from the pillow-shaped boulder standing in a field. Shawn keeps the name. He left a Methodist seminary and then spent twenty years arguing that dance is worship, and he has bought a farm named after the stone Jacob slept on. There is a photograph of him with his head laid on the boulder.

stops.campa: Barton Mumaw, nineteen, from Eustis in Florida, has been following Shawn since seeing a Denishawn performance the year before. At the farm he becomes the household's other permanent inhabitant, the company's star soloist, and Shawn's lover, and stays roughly seventeen years. Shawn is married and remains married. The arrangement holds through the whole life of the Men Dancers. Nobody in the period says any of it in print; the dancers know, and the Berkshire neighbours mostly do not.

stops.campa: Shawn teaches at Springfield College, an all-male school built on muscular Christianity and physical education, and recruits its athletes into a dance company. They arrive able to lift, hold and fall, and not able to dance. He trains them from nothing. The premise is a wager about the American male body: that men in work clothes, doing something that looks like labour, can be watched dancing by audiences who would jeer a man in tights. Mumaw, who came to him from Florida rather than from this campus, dances at the head of them.
stops.quote: I wanted to see if the American man in plain brown pants and a bare torso could speak profound things.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, quoted in James B. Simpson, Simpson's Contemporary Quotations, pp. 344-45, from a press item of 21 August 1964; the underlying periodical could not be resolved and the attribution is carried as reconstruction

stops.campa: On the fourteenth of July 1933 Ted Shawn and His Men Dancers give the performance from which the Jacob's Pillow festival counts itself continuous. The audience sits on benches the dancers built. They have spent the preceding weeks clearing land and repairing farm buildings, and they will put up most of the structures on the property with their own hands between tours for the next seven years. The Friday teas leading up to this cost seventy-five cents. The first one drew fifty-seven people onto seating built for twenty-five.

stops.name: Becket: Kinetic Molpai
stops.date_confidence: The 1935 premiere comes from the research dossier's citation of the Jacob's Pillow Dance Interactive film catalogue, which could not be independently re-fetched; the same archive is cited on Wikipedia, 'Ted Shawn' for a restored 1937 film of the work, and the two dates are left unreconciled here. The month is unknown and defaulted. Mumaw's 1992 return to teach the piece is attested by Wikipedia, 'Ted Shawn'; it is his own later act and is carried in this campa and in suggested_refs as a source on Shawn's stop, not staged as a scene of its own.
stops.campa: Shawn premieres Kinetic Molpai on the Men Dancers, an abstract ensemble work in a sequence of movements with no story, no country and no costume beyond trunks. The title is his own coinage from a Greek word for a choral dance. It does what the Asian repertory never quite did: it stops depicting anybody and drives a group of men through force and recovery. It survives on film, and in 1992 Barton Mumaw comes back to the Pillow to teach it to dancers who never saw Shawn alive. The premiere is dated 1935 and the restored film 1937, and the two have not been reconciled.
stops.quote: To get back to fundamentals, the reason the dance of America is succeeding is because it has gone back to first principles and realized that unless we dance from our own God-consciousness, from the center of our being, unless we express through the medium of the dance the highest and finest thing of which we are capable, the most cosmic thing that we can conceive, we will merely be imitating and following in the path of the dying systems of the older nations.
stops.quote_source: Ted Shawn, The American Ballet (1926), nine years before the premiere

stops.name: Becket: the letter about defenseless boys

stops.campa: On the eleventh of August 1939 Ruth St. Denis writes her estranged husband five angry pages. She accuses him of drawing to himself defenseless boys who come looking for friendship or for mothering and who find instead, in her phrase, an impossible lover. They have been apart eight years and married twenty-five. The letter survives in an archive. It is the only surviving statement of what she thought of the household at Becket, and nothing in the record indicates that he answered it.

stops.campa: On the thirty-first of August 1940 Ted Shawn and His Men Dancers give their final homecoming performance and the company ends. Seven years, a punishing touring schedule, most of the buildings on the property raised by the men who danced in them. The war is coming and the dancers will be in it. Shawn is forty-eight, out of a company for the second time in ten years, and some twenty thousand dollars in debt on a farm he is considering selling. He leases it out instead, to a dance teacher named Mary Washington Ball, whose season there does not pay.

stops.date_confidence: The 1954 publication of Every Little Movement is confirmed by the OpenLibrary catalogue record (Pittsfield and Brooklyn, 1954, with Dance Horizons reprints from 1968), as is the French edition Chaque petit mouvement, published in Brussels by Editions Complexe in 2005; the research pool had that translation flagged as unconfirmed and it can be upgraded. stops.campa: Shawn publishes Every Little Movement, a study of François Delsarte, the Frenchman who died in 1871 having charted the correspondences between gesture and inner state and having never taught a dancer. Shawn had been given the Delsarte system at second hand, through Ruth St. Denis and her mother, before he could name what it was; the book is him going back to find where his own vocabulary came from. It is reprinted for decades and translated into French in Brussels in 2005, thirty-three years after his death.

stops.name: Becket: Inge Sand steps in

stops.campa: The Danish ballerina Inge Sand makes her United States debut at the Pillow on short notice, bringing August Bournonville's choreography before an American audience for the first time. Shawn, who spent his youth being told that American dance was a contradiction in terms, has built the platform on which a foreign classical tradition now enters the country. The festival is no longer his company's home; it is a house that programmes other people. Whether he meant it to become one is not something he is on record saying.
